extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in introductory discrete mathematics / proofs (functions, set theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for defining, reasoning about, and proving properties of functions (domain/codomain/range, injective/surjective/bijective, composition, inverses, image/preimage, pigeonhole, cardinality). Aimed at students doing exercises and formal proofs in an introductory undergraduate course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-theoretic definition of a function
rubrics_metrics.description: Any function f : A → B is a subset of A × B. (Contrast with informal 'rule' view; the set definition removes ambiguity.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook emphasizes thinking of a function as a set of ordered pairs rather than a nebulous 'rule'. While in practice we may think of f(x)=|x|+2 as a rule, rigorous arguments should rely on the set notation. Examples: f = {(1,a),(2,a),(3,b)}. Anti-pattern: relying only on informal 'rule' language when domain/codomain issues matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain, codomain, and range (image) distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain is the set A of allowed inputs; codomain is B; range (image) is the set of actual outputs {f(x): x∈A}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly reminds readers that surjectivity is equivalent to 'codomain equals range'. Exercises and examples illustrate computing domain, codomain and range from an explicit set of pairs or formula. Watch for confusion between f({a}) vs f(a) and between image f(X) and element f(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two functions f : A → B and g : C → D are equal if A = C, B = D, and f(x) = g(x) for every x ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important subtlety: identical formulas do not guarantee equality if codomains differ. Example: f: Z→N and g: Z→Z defined by same rule may not be equal because codomains differ. To prove equality check domains, codomains, and pointwise equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injective (one-to-one) — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : A → B is injective if for every x,y ∈ A, x ≠ y implies f(x) ≠ f(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual intuition: distinct elements in A map to distinct elements in B. Equivalently, f(x)=f(y) ⇒ x=y (contrapositive form). Example: x^3 on R is injective; x^2 is not. Anti-pattern: confusing injectivity with surjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjective (onto) — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : A → B is surjective if for every b ∈ B there exists an a ∈ A with f(a) = b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, the range equals the codomain. Proof technique: start with an arbitrary b∈B and produce an a (solve f(a)=b or give construction). Example: x^3 on R is surjective; x^2: R→R is not (negative numbers not in range). To disprove surjectivity, provide a b∈B with no preimage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijective — definition and consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: f is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bijective functions have inverses; bijection = perfect one-to-one correspondence between domain and codomain. Practice: show bijectivity by proving injectivity and surjectivity separately or by constructing an explicit inverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques to prove injectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct approach: suppose x,y∈A and x≠y; deduce f(x)≠f(y). Contrapositive approach: suppose f(x)=f(y); deduce x=y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text recommends the contrapositive is often easiest when f is given by an algebraic formula, because equations are easier to manipulate than inequalities. Provide worked examples (e.g., use contrapositive to show g(m,n)=(m+n,m+2n) is injective).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show a function is not injective
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove injectivity, find explicit x≠y in A such that f(x)=f(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single counterexample suffices. Examples shown: f(x)=x^2 is not injective because f(-2)=f(2). Antipattern: attempting an existential disproof by indirect means when a concrete counterexample is simpler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques to prove surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f : A → B is surjective, suppose b∈B and prove there exists a∈A with f(a)=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches include solving the equation f(a)=b for a (algebraic inversion) or constructing a based on common sense. Example: for g: Z×Z→Z×Z with g(m,n)=(m+n,m+2n), solve the linear system to find preimage (x,y) for arbitrary (b,c).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show a function is not surjective
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove surjectivity, prove the negation: there exists b∈B such that for all a∈A, f(a) ≠ b (i.e., b has no preimage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often this is done by identifying an element of the codomain not in the range. Example: f(x)=x^2 on R is not surjective onto R because negative numbers have no preimage. Keep in mind formal negation of '∀b ∃a' is '∃b ∀a'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole Principle (finite sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A and B are finite sets and f : A → B is any function. Then: (1) If |A| > |B|, f is not injective. (2) If |A| < |B|, f is not surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a counting-based proof technique: e.g., show among 10 integers 1–100 there exist distinct subsets with equal sums by mapping subsets to sums and applying pigeonhole. Visual and combinatorial examples illustrate application. Anti-pattern: applying pigeonhole incorrectly to infinite sets without modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of functions — definition and domain/codomain constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and g : B → C (codomain of f equals domain of g), the composition g∘f : A → C is defined by g∘f(x) = g(f(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with order: g∘f means apply f first, then g. Composition also makes sense if range(f) ⊆ domain(g); textbook emphasizes codomain equality for simplicity. Example: if codomain/domain mismatch (B ≠ C) composition may be undefined. Anti-pattern: assuming composition is commutative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition is not commutative but is associative
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when g∘f and f∘g are both defined, they need not be equal (composition not commutative). Theorem: composition is associative: (h∘g)∘f = h∘(g∘f) when types line up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: evaluate both sides on arbitrary x and reduce to h(g(f(x))). Use associativity in chain compositions in proofs. Example provided in textbook with formulas showing g∘f and f∘g differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves injectivity and surjectivity under conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and g : B → C are both injective then g∘f is injective. If both f and g are surjective then g∘f is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategies: for injective case, assume g∘f(x)=g∘f(y) and deduce x=y via injectivity of g then f. For surjective case, given c∈C find b∈B with g(b)=c and a∈A with f(a)=b. Note: composition of two bijections is bijection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation and when it is a function
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a relation R from A to B, the inverse relation R^{-1} = {(y,x) : (x,y)∈R} is a relation from B to A. For a function f, f^{-1} (as a relation) is a function iff f is bijective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If f is bijective then f^{-1} is a function from B to A and obeys f^{-1}∘f = i_A and f∘f^{-1} = i_B. If f fails to be injective or surjective, its inverse relation either fails to be a function (duplicates first coordinates) or isn't total (missing first coordinates). Examples illustrate both failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing inverses (algebraic method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: write y = f(x), interchange variables to x = f(y), solve for y to obtain y = f^{-1}(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this when f is given by an algebraic formula and invertible. Check by composing f^{-1}(f(x)) = x. Examples: invert x^3+1 and linear transformations on Z×Z via solving systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity function — definition and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For set A the identity function i_A : A → A is defined by i_A(x) = x for every x∈A. i_A is bijective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identities serve as neutral elements for composition; used when proving f^{-1}∘f = i_A etc. Examples: i_{ {1,2,3} } = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image (f(X)) and preimage (f^{-1}(Y)) — definitions and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊆ A then f(X) = {f(x): x∈X} ⊆ B. If Y ⊆ B then f^{-1}(Y) = {x∈A : f(x)∈Y} ⊆ A. (These definitions apply even when f is not invertible.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between f^{-1} as preimage operator on sets and f^{-1} as inverse function (exists only when f is bijective). Examples show f^{-1}( {4} ) = {s,x,z} even if f^{-1} function does not exist. Note: f(f^{-1}(Y)) ⊆ Y in general; X ⊆ f^{-1}(f(X)) always holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-theoretic properties of images and preimages (Theorem 12.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some equalities fail in general (e.g., f(W∩X)=f(W)∩f(X) need not hold); produce counterexamples when false. Exercises ask to prove inclusions and exhibit counterexamples. Use these rules when manipulating images/preimages in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality via bijections (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets A and B have the same cardinality, written |A| = |B|, if there exists a bijective function f : A → B. If no bijection exists, |A| ≠ |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to finite and infinite sets. Examples: exhibit explicit bijection N → Z to show |N| = |Z|. Emphasize bijection construction as proof technique for equal cardinalities; injective or surjective-only functions are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonal argument (non-surjectivity of N→R)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantor's diagonalization constructs a real number differing in the nth decimal place from f(n) for an arbitrary purported surjection f : N → R, showing no such surjection exists (thus |N| ≠ |R|).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text presents the diagonal-band idea and specific digit-choice rule (choose 6 if the diagonal digit ≠6, else choose 2) to build a number not in the image. Use this to prove uncountability of reals and to reason about different sizes of infinity.
